author: @FrankCurzio
text:
Microsoft offered 60,000 employees the exit while it pours billions into AI.

Now Outlook has been down for almost a full day.

I warned about this a few days ago, and half a million of you read it. AI is an incredible tool, but this is what happens when you get it wrong.

Absolute circus - here's what happened...

Thursday morning in the US, Outlook stopped opening for people in more than 70 countries. Teams and Copilot went down with it.

Microsoft says it wasn't a hack. It says its servers became "unexpectedly unavailable," and some it brought back online failed again overnight.

Almost a full day later, it's still rolling back changes and can't say when everything will be fixed.

Meanwhile, its CEO is talking about 20 million AI agents doing the work, and analysts say a lot of Microsoft's experienced engineers have already left.

I'm still buying the companies building out AI... that trade isn't going anywhere because the orders are already locked in. 

But the companies betting they can swap their best people for AI are going to keep learning this the hard way.
quoted_text:
It looks like the AI layoff boom has started to backfire.

I was just going through a Reuters investigation on Meta, and holy shit...

They drew up plans to cut some teams by as much as 60% and let AI agents do the work. THEN Zuckerberg called off the next round of layoffs hours before the first one even started.

And when you look at the numbers... they tell you why.

Engineers were pushing out 220% more code, BUT major technical and security incidents jumped 40%.

So people spent 70% more time putting out fires.

AI cranked out way more work, and humans spent way more time cleaning it up.

A different report I saw this week showed something similar.

32% of hiring managers said they brought back the exact jobs they cut for AI.

Think about how dumb that is. You fire people, pay a fortune for AI, then pay again to hire the same people back.

Look, I’m no AI bear. I use AI every single day.

It saves me a shit ton of time and I’m not going back. It’s an incredible tool.

But market forces are still market forces.

Every boom in history has been overhyped, and every CEO wanted to stand up and tell Wall Street he could do more with half the people.

Now from what I’m seeing, reality is kicking in.

It costs way more than they thought, it breaks shit, and you still need people who know what the hell they’re doing.

Even the AI companies are feeling it. Elon just cut Grok’s usage limits and admitted it costs more to run than it brings in.

I still think AI is a great bet, and I’m still buying the companies building the data centers. But you need balance, and the guys who went all in on firing everyone are learning that the hard way.

Be careful out there.

author: @FrankCurzio
text:
BREAKING: SpaceX will try to catch both halves of its Starship rocket today, a first.

The booster flies back to the launch tower in Texas minutes after liftoff. That part has worked 3 times.

The upper stage is new. It comes home about 22 hours later and has never been caught.

Musk calls success "more likely than not."

Rockets cost a fortune because most of the hardware gets thrown away after every flight, so catching both halves and flying them again makes a launch look more like an airline trip.

This one carries 26 Starlink satellites.

SpaceX is its own first customer.

A great catch still doesn't make me a buyer of SpaceX ($SPCX). Share unlocks are ahead & Democrats are coming after Musk.

Verizon and AT&T dividend holders should care more than Musk fans. Cheaper launches put up more satellites competing with the airwaves those carriers own.

author: @rubicon59
text: Greedy capitalists taking advantage of Texas.
quoted_text:
SpaceX is building a supercomputer near Brownsville, Texas.

The first job on site was cleaning up sixty years of other people's trash.

Scrap metal, rusting tanks, old appliances and thousands of illegal tires, hauled out of the mud.

Think about that for a second.

This site will train frontier AI for medical research, emergency response, advanced manufacturing and national security.

It will make its own electricity, so the neighbors' power bills stay their own.

SpaceX is also putting $220 million into Brownsville's water and wastewater system, adding 20 million gallons of capacity every day for the city.

More than 3,000 construction jobs already, with more than 500 permanent ones to come.

Elon Musk summed it up in three words: "SpaceX community benefits."

A company spends $15 billion on Starship and another $24 billion on a supercomputer in one corner of Texas when it plans to stay for decades.

Elon Musk builds the place up first, because he believes the future will be built right there.
